# Two Rings

For two years after my mother died, I called her telephone every Sunday at eleven.

Not to talk. To listen. It would ring twice — that patient double pulse I'd known all my life, her phone rattling the hall table in the house I grew up in — and then her voice: *You've reached Eleanor. Leave what you've got after the beep, and don't skimp on the details. Details are the good part.* A little laugh on the end. She'd recorded it in 2009, sitting on the edge of the bathtub because the acoustics were better in there, and she thought she sounded silly, and she didn't, and I never told her so, because telling her would have meant admitting I'd noticed.

I never stayed for the beep. I'd hang up in the small silence after the laugh, before the tone, so the call would register as nothing — a wrong number, a pocket dial, a ghost with good manners.

The greeting was younger than she'd been at the end. In it she still had the voice of the woman who drove carpool with the windows down, who sang harmony to the radio slightly wrong on purpose, just to make me correct her. At the end, her voice had gone thin as paper. But the machine kept the other one, the sturdy one, and on Sundays I borrowed it.

People suggested I copy the recording onto my computer. There are services for this, apparently. But a copy felt like taxidermy, and the call felt like a visit. You can't visit a file.

I knew it couldn't last. The dead don't pay phone bills, so I did — I'd kept the account open, and every month I paid it like a subscription to a small miracle. Real voices called to offer me upgrades. I declined. I didn't want her number improved. I wanted it exactly as it was: two rings, one greeting, one laugh, hanging in the world like a light left on in a window.

Two years is a hundred and four Sundays. I called from grocery-store parking lots and hotel rooms, from a hospital waiting room where a nurse assumed I was confirming my ride home. Once, during a thunderstorm, the line crackled and I panicked — absurdly, privately — as if weather could get into the recording and rot it. It wasn't that I'd forgotten she was gone. It was that the greeting didn't know yet, and I wasn't ready to be the one to tell it.

Then, on a Sunday in March, with the early light doing its trick of looking like hope, I called, and a man answered.

"Hello?" he said. "Hello?"

I should have hung up. What was there to say — sorry, I was expecting a dead woman? But grief makes you selfish in the smallest ways, and I heard myself ask whether the phone had come with a greeting.

A pause. "The voicemail thing? Yeah. *You've reached Eleanor* — I figured it was broken. Some old leftover. I was going to have it removed."

"It's not broken," I said. "It's my mother." And, because he deserved more than that: "She died two years ago. The greeting is the only recording I have of her voice. Every Sunday I call, listen, hang up. I never thought anyone would pick up."

Somewhere behind him a child was demanding something with the full conviction of the very young. He said "hold on" — not to me — and the phone muffled against his shirt, and I sat in my kitchen and understood I was about to lose her a second time: not to death, which had at least left her number standing, but to a stranger's housekeeping. Someone was always going to erase her. It might as well be today.

When he came back he said, "I switched carriers last month. The message came over with the number somehow. Before they wipe it, I—" Papers shuffled. "I wrote it down. Word for word. Should I read it to you?"

A greeting read off a stranger's transcription is not a greeting. It's a eulogy with the wrong eulogist. But my mother raised me to believe you never turn down the offer of a voice, so I said yes.

He cleared his throat. "*You've reached Eleanor. Leave what you've got after the beep, and don't skimp on the details. Details are the good part.*" He stopped where the laugh went, and in the pause I supplied it myself, note for note — the small *hah* she tucked onto the end of her own jokes, because she believed you should laugh at them first, so no one could beat you to it.

"That's her," I said. I was crying in the bright kitchen, and it was fine. It was Sunday. That was allowed.

"She sounds like a nice lady," he said.

"She was slow to return calls. Impossible about the thermostat. She harmonized wrong on purpose." I wiped my face with the dish towel. "Thank you. You didn't have to do any of that."

"I'll leave the message on," he said. "It sounds better in there anyway. And if you ever want to stay for the beep — I won't listen. I'd just delete them."

I stayed exactly once, that first week. Talked for four minutes about nothing: the thermostat, the March light, a man with a child and a promise. Then I hung up gently, the way you close a door in a house you're leaving in better shape than you found it.

That night I sat on the edge of my own bathtub — the acoustics really are better in there — and recorded a new outgoing message: *You've reached Eleanor's daughter. Leave what you've got after the beep, and don't skimp on the details. Details are the good part.* Then I laughed at the end, so no one could beat me to it.

**Two Rings**

For two years after my mother died, I called her telephone every Sunday at eleven.

Not to talk. To listen. It rang twice — that patient double pulse I'd known all my life, her phone rattling the hall table in the house I grew up in — and then her voice: *You've reached Eleanor. Leave what you've got after the beep, and don't skimp on the details. Details are the good part.* A little laugh at the end. She recorded it in 2009, sitting on the edge of the bathtub because the acoustics were better in there, and she thought she sounded silly, and she didn't, and I never told her so, because telling her would have meant admitting I'd noticed.

I never stayed for the beep. I'd hang up in the small silence after the laugh, before the tone, so the call would register as nothing — a wrong number, a pocket dial, a ghost with good manners.

The greeting was younger than she'd been at the end. In it she still had the voice of the woman who drove carpool with the windows down, who sang harmony to the radio slightly wrong on purpose just to make me correct her. At the end her voice had gone thin as paper. But the machine kept the other one, the sturdy one, and on Sundays I borrowed it.

I knew it couldn't last. The dead don't pay phone bills, so I did — I'd kept the account, and every month I paid it like a subscription to a small miracle. Customer-service voices offered me upgrades. I declined. I didn't want her number upgraded. I wanted it exactly as it was: two rings, one greeting, one laugh, burning in the world like a light left on in a window.

Then, on a Sunday in March, with the early light doing its trick of looking like hope, I called and a man answered.

"Hello?" he said. "Hello?"

I should have hung up. What was there to say — sorry, I was expecting a dead woman? But grief makes you selfish in the smallest ways, and I heard myself ask whether the phone had come with a greeting.

A pause. "The voicemail thing? Yeah. *You've reached Eleanor* — I figured it was broken. Some old leftover. I was going to have it removed."

"It's not broken," I said. "It's my mother." And, because he deserved more than that: "She died two years ago. The greeting is the only recording I have of her voice. Every Sunday I call and listen and hang up. I never thought anyone would answer."

Somewhere behind him, a child was demanding something with the full conviction of the very young. He said "hold on" — not to me — and the phone muffled against his shirt, and I sat in my kitchen and understood that I was about to lose her a second time: not to death, which had at least left her number intact, but to a stranger's housekeeping. Someone was always going to erase her. It might as well be today.

When he came back, he said, "I switched carriers last month. The message survived the transfer, somehow. Before they wipe it, I—" Papers shuffled. "I wrote it down. Word for word. Should I read it to you?"

A greeting read off a stranger's transcription is not a greeting. It's a eulogy with the wrong eulogist. But my mother raised me to believe you never turn down the offer of a voice, so I said yes.

He cleared his throat. "*You've reached Eleanor. Leave what you've got after the beep, and don't skimp on the details. Details are the good part.*" He stopped where the laugh went, and in that pause I supplied it myself, note for note — the small *hah* she tucked onto the end of her own jokes, because she believed you should laugh first, so nobody could beat you to it.

"That's her," I said. I was crying in the bright kitchen, and it was fine. It was Sunday. That was allowed.

"She sounds like a nice lady," he said.

"She was slow to return calls. Impossible about the thermostat. She harmonized wrong on purpose." I wiped my face on the dish towel. "Thank you. You didn't have to do any of that."

"I'll leave the message on," he said. "It sounds better anyway. You could — if you ever wanted to stay for the beep, I wouldn't listen. I'd just delete them."

That night I sat on the edge of my own bathtub — the acoustics really are better in there — and recorded a new outgoing message: *You've reached [my name]. Leave what you've got after the beep, and don't skimp on the details. Details are the good part.* Then I laughed at the end, so no one could beat me to it.

I still call some Sundays, at eleven. Two rings, her voice, the laugh. And once — just once — I stayed for the tone and talked for four minutes about nothing: the thermostat, the light in March, a man with a child and a promise. When I finished, the machine said goodbye in its flat way, and I hung up first, gently, the way you close a door in a house you're leaving to someone else.
